title: The Quiet Signals of Product-Market Fit
transcript:
Jordan Vance: Priya, you're back. Last time we talked about activation. Today I want to talk about a question every early-stage founder asks: how do you actually know if you have product-market fit, before the revenue numbers make it obvious?

Priya Chandrasekaran: The revenue numbers are a lagging indicator, they tell you what already happened months ago. The signals I trust show up in behavior long before they show up in a board deck. The first one is unprompted usage intensity: are people using the product more than you expected without you nudging them, versus using it exactly as much as your onboarding emails tell them to. If usage tracks your marketing calendar instead of the customer's own needs, that's a warning sign, not a fit signal.

Jordan Vance: What's a second signal?

Priya Chandrasekaran: How people describe the product to others when you're not in the room. Not NPS surveys, actual language. When we had real fit at one company, customers started describing us using a metaphor we hadn't invented ourselves, they'd say it's like having a second brain for scheduling, and that phrase started showing up in support tickets and in sales calls from prospects who'd talked to existing customers. When you don't have fit yet, customers describe you using your own marketing copy back at you, which means they've adopted your language but not necessarily your value.

Jordan Vance: That's a subtle distinction. How do you check for it deliberately?

Priya Chandrasekaran: I read every piece of unsolicited customer language I can find, support tickets, community posts, sales call transcripts, and I specifically look for phrases that don't appear anywhere in our own website or emails. If I can't find any, either we don't have fit yet, or we haven't shipped anything distinctive enough for people to need new language to describe it.

Jordan Vance: What's a signal people misread as fit when it isn't?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Rapid signup growth from a single channel, especially a paid channel or a well-executed launch. That measures your ability to get attention, not your ability to deliver value once attention arrives. I've watched teams celebrate a launch day spike and then quietly bleed those same users over the following month, because the spike tested distribution, not fit. The real test is always what a cohort does eight, twelve, sixteen weeks after acquisition, once the initial novelty and any launch excitement has fully worn off.

Jordan Vance: If someone listening is unsure whether they have fit, what should they check this week?

Priya Chandrasekaran: Pull your signup cohorts from three and four months ago and look at what fraction are still doing the core action weekly, not just logging in. Then go read the last thirty pieces of unsolicited customer language you can find and count how many phrases aren't yours. Those two things together tell you more than any survey.
